title: Attention kernel optimization profiling: FlashAttention, paged attention, fused ops
content:
Summary:
We ran a focused profiling investigation comparing popular attention kernel strategies used in the serving runtime: FlashAttention (v1/v2), paged attention (KV paging to avoid large KV cache resident memory), and fused QKV/QKVOps. The goal was to identify bottlenecks (compute vs memory vs kernel-launch overhead), failure modes at low-latency/high-concurrency operating points, and concrete optimizations we can apply in the next quarter.

High-level findings:
- FlashAttention (v2) gives the best token throughput and lower memory bandwidth pressure for long sequence lengths (>=1024) on A100/MI250 when the implementation and kernel tiling match our sequence shapes.
- Paged attention reduces peak GPU memory and allows larger context by moving parts of KV to host or staging buffers; however, it introduces extra CPU/GPU synchronization and can suffer at low-latency (per-request) workloads due to added copy overheads.
- Fused ops (QKV fusion, fused softmax + dropout + matmul when possible) reduce kernel-launch overhead and reduce global memory traffic; benefits are largest for small batch sizes and short sequences where kernel launch overhead dominates.

Goals for this doc:
- Document reproducible profiling methodology used in experiments.
- Surface where the runtime is currently limited for each kernel strategy.
- Recommend targeted optimizations and follow-up experiments.

Environment and test harness:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 40GB (PCIe) and NVIDIA H100 (selected spots), also run smoke checks on RTX6000 for dev reproducibility.
- OS / Drivers: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8 (A100) / CUDA 12.1 (H100 for compatibility tests), NVIDIA driver 535+.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch: feature/attention-ker-profiling (commit a1b2c3d), torch 2.3.0 + custom aten kernels for fused ops.
- Model: Open-architecture GPT-like model (decoder-only) converted to optimized runtime format. Tests run with sequence lengths: 128, 512, 1024, 2048 and batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 to capture PLG and batch-serving modes.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec (throughput), GPU utilization (nvidia-smi & Nsight GPU), SM efficiency, achieved memory bandwidth, L2 hit rates (from Nsight), kernel-level time breakdown (Nsight Systems / nvprof / Nsight Compute).

Methodology (reproducible steps):
1) Start a single-node serving runtime with pinned model and warm-up 300 tokens per run to stabilize caches.
2) Use bench harness (bench/attention_bench.py) that issues either single-request streaming (PLG-simulated) or micro-batched requests and records per-token latencies.
3) Profiling commands (examples):
   - Nsight Systems (system-wide timeline): nsys profile -o profile.nsys --trace=cuda,osrt python -m bench.attention_bench --kernel flashattention --seq 1024 --batch 4
   - Nsight Compute (kernel metrics): ncu --set full -o ncu_report --target-processes all python -m bench.attention_bench --kernel flashattention --seq 1024 --batch 4
   - Lightweight sampling for production-like runs: CUPTI-based telemetry in tracing pipeline, plus runtime counters emitted to observability.
4) For paged attention, enable kv-paging flags in runtime and run with staging configured to host pinned memory and a 1 ms copy budget for page-in. Collect extra traces for CPU memcpy and NVMe if used.

Kernels tested and variants:
- flashattention-v1 (reference)
- flashattention-v2 (improved tiling and mixed-precision kernels)
- paged-attention-host-pinned (KV pages in pinned host mem)
- paged-attention-device-staging (KV pages staged on GPU but swapped to smaller fragments)
- fused-qkv + fused-softmax (inlined QKV projection + attention matmul + softmax fused kernels)
- baseline naive attention (for comparison)

Representative results (summary tables — numbers are medians from 5 runs):
- Seq=128, Batch=1: fused-qkv best p99 latency (12.5ms), flashatt-V2 (14.2ms), paged-attention (20.8ms)
- Seq=1024, Batch=4: flashatt-V2 best throughput (tokens/sec 78k), fused ops similar throughput but +8% memory use, paged-attention reduces peak mem by ~45% with throughput hit ~30%
- Seq=2048, Batch=1 (long context single-request): flashatt-V2 stable, paged-attention allows the run to complete (baseline OOM), latency 1.4x higher than in-memory flashatt-V2.

Key profiling observations by kernel:
1) FlashAttention (v2)
   - Kernel-level: higher SM occupancy and higher sustained tensor core utilization.
   - Memory: lower L2 bandwidth due to more compute per byte; effective for long sequences.
   - Overheads: single large kernels can run for many ms which compresses kernel launch overhead but means a single stuck kernel matters more for preemption.
   - Failure modes: sequence length mismatch vs kernel tiling can cause suboptimal occupancy (e.g., seq=1536 on some configs).

2) Paged attention
   - Kernel-level: smaller kernels operating on page-sized KV windows; extra memcpy kernels visible in timeline.
   - CPU/GPU sync: page faulting or on-demand page-in causes spikes in tail latency; host-pinned copies cost ~0.6-2.5ms depending on page size and copy path.
   - Benefit: enables contexts that would otherwise OOM; good for batch workloads tolerant of per-request variability (e.g., offline indexing).
   - Bottleneck: copy bandwidth + API sync; need async copy + overlap to mitigate.

3) Fused ops
   - Launch overhead: reduced number of kernels per attention pass; measured 20–35% latency reduction at batch sizes 1–4 for short sequences.
   - Memory traffic: fewer loads/stores; improves register reuse and L1/L2 locality.
   - Tradeoffs: increased register pressure; on some older GPUs this reduced occupancy and offset gains. Requires per-GPU autotuning.

Profiling artifacts and micro-examples (commands + sample snippets):
- Nsight Systems timeline showed significant time spent in cudaMemcpyAsync + cudaStreamSynchronize for paged-attention. Suggests we are not fully overlapping copies with compute.
- ncu kernel report for flashatt-v2 shows warps issued: 98% occupancy, achieved tensor core utilization 87%, DRAM throughput 60% of theoretical.
- For fused ops, ncu indicated increased register usage per thread (reg usage +30) which reduced occupancy from 80% -> 62% on A100; despite that, latency improved due to fewer global memory roundtrips.

Immediate recommendations (quarter roadmap):
1) Integrate FlashAttention v2 variant as primary long-context kernel path behind a feature flag; add automatic kernel selector based on sequence length and hardware capability.
2) Implement async KV page prefetcher in runtime: speculative prefetch for adjacent pages + overlapping device copies with compute using multiple streams to hide copy latency.
3) Add per-GPU autotuner that picks optimal tiling/fusion parameters (register tiling, block size) at first model load; cache results in model metadata.
4) Expose kernel-level telemetry in Redwood Console (per-route kernel breakdown) so we can tie regressions to kernel changes and A/B models.
5) For fused ops, add GPU-specific fallbacks: if reg pressure reduces occupancy below threshold, revert to less-fused variant.

Longer-term research ideas:
- Explore a hybrid scheduler that routes low-latency single-request traffic to fused-op optimized stacks and high-throughput long-context traffic to FlashAttention optimized stacks.
- Kernel-level autotuning with ML-based cost model to predict throughput/latency given batch/seq shapes.
- Investigate NVLink peer-to-peer staging for environments with multi-GPU per-request contexts to avoid host hops for KV pages.

Open action items (owners):
- Miguel Torres: prototype async KV prefetch implementation + microbench (target end of sprint).
- Priya Patel: run full sweep across fleet GPUs (A100/H100) and collect ncu reports for seq in {128,512,1024,2048}.
- Samir Gupta: implement FlashAttention v2 switch + unit tests, add kernel selector heuristics.
- Avery Chen (me): create instrumentation emission spec for Console and add event schemas.

Appendix - useful commands and notes:
- Run bench harness: python -m bench.attention_bench --model redwood-gpt-small --kernel flashattention-v2 --seq 1024 --batch 4 --warmup 300 --tokens 5000
- Nsight Systems: nsys profile -o /tmp/attn.nsys --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=none python -m bench.attention_bench --kernel paged-attention --seq 2048
- Nsight Compute example: ncu --set full -o /tmp/ncu_flash_v2 --target-processes all python -m bench.attention_bench --kernel flashattention-v2 --seq 1024
- Microtrace to capture host<->device copy timings: enable runtime flag --trace-copy-kv and look for events tagged PAGE_PREFETCH_START / PAGE_PREFETCH_DONE in trace.

Notes / open questions to discuss in next sync:
- What are our SLO/latency budgets per offering (hosted vs dedicated) for long context workloads? That will drive whether we prioritize paged-attention or force customers to Dedicated with more GPU memory.
- Should we gate paged-attention behind Dedicated-only to avoid tail latency surprises in hosted PLG?
- How to expose cost tradeoffs to customers (token cost vs memory vs latency) in Console so they can choose a preferred kernel policy.

Please review and add any missing experiments or observations. I will attach ncu/nsys artifacts to the Confluence page and link PRs as they land.

-- Avery
